claims.text: Precise control of nucleation kinetics promotes atomic-level mixing of noble metals in high-entropy alloy nanomaterials.
Atomic-level mixing establishes a uniform distribution of catalytically active sites.
A uniform distribution of active sites governs reliable material formation and enhances catalytic performance.
Controlled heating and slow cooling slow the nucleation and growth stages relative to rapid synthesis.
At 300–500°C under inert or reducing atmospheres, thermodynamic equilibrium can be approached gradually.
Nanoscale imaging and surface compositional analyses can verify the degree of atomic-level intermixing and alloy uniformity.
Slower, controlled nucleation produces a more homogeneous distribution of noble metals in the alloy matrix.
A more homogeneous noble-metal distribution reduces local compositional fluctuations.
Greater compositional uniformity increases the number and accessibility of catalytically active sites.
Greater compositional uniformity minimizes the formation of less-active segregated phases.
Controlled-nucleation materials will have higher conversion rates or turnover frequencies than rapidly synthesized materials.
Controlled-nucleation materials will exhibit more consistent catalytic performance than rapidly synthesized materials.
Rapid nucleation and cooling are likely to produce less-uniform atomic distributions and lower catalytic performance.
The proposed relationship should hold when thermal energy and cooling rates permit gradual nucleation.
The relationship may fail when temperature or atmosphere causes kinetic factors to prevent equilibrium-driven atomic mixing.
No direct prior experimental evidence for noble-metal high-entropy alloys under the specified controlled synthesis conditions is present in the provided records.
